1.title: Governing Deployment and Use
1.text: Welcome to Module thirteen: Governing Deployment and Use. This is the largest competency of domain four. It follows the deployer from the first user to the final shutdown: policies and training, monitoring, periodic checks, records, unintended uses, communication, and the policy to switch a system off or limit it.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do seven things. Apply policies, practices and ethics to a system in use. Run monitoring, and a schedule of maintenance, updates and retraining, from the deployer's side. Carry out periodic checks. Keep records of incidents, issues, risks and monitoring plans. Forecast and reduce secondary and unintended uses and their downstream harm. Set up external communication plans. And put in place the policy and controls to switch a system off or limit it by region.

1.title: Case Check-In: Oversight, a Misused Assistant and a Switched-Off Feature
1.text: At Helios, Lucia Moreno's recruiters review the hiring tool's ranking before any decision, and the oversight must be real, not a rubber stamp. A recruiter uses the customer assistant to rank résumés, a use it was never approved for. Samira Haddad asks for an external communication plan for the assistant and the hiring tool. And the emotion-analysis feature is switched off in the E U and limited by region elsewhere. Your task: govern the two systems while they are in use.

1.title: Deployment Governance: Policies, Procedures and Roles
1.text: Putting a system into use means applying the organization's policies, from module three, not writing new ones. The figure shows six elements. A named owner: one accountable business owner. Procedures: a deployment checklist, change control and escalation. Then four practices that run through use: user training, issue management, data governance and risk management. Ethics matter too: the values and red lines in the policy decide what the system may be used for. At Helios, Lucia Moreno owns the hiring tool and Anika Berg owns the assistant. Exam tip: policies exist before deployment; deployment governance applies them.

1.title: Data Governance and Risk Management in Use
1.text: In use, the deployer controls what goes in. For a high-risk system it must ensure input data are relevant and sufficiently representative, under Article twenty-six. Set rules for users: what may be entered, and where outputs may go. Give knowledge sources owners, review dates and versions. Respect privacy: retention limits, access control and a lawful basis. And keep risk management alive: the risk register is updated from monitoring, feedback and incidents, not left at its launch version. At Helios, the support documents get owners and review dates after the wrong refund answer. Exam tip: the risk register stays alive.

1.title: Issue Management: From Report to Fix
1.text: An issue is a problem found in use: a wrong output, a complaint, a workaround or a gap in a document. Give users and affected people an easy way to report, with an owner who reads it. The flow is: log, triage by severity, assign, fix, verify and close. An issue that causes or could cause harm moves to the incident process from module ten. Repeated issues point to a systemic cause and go to the committee. N I S T Govern five point one asks policies to collect and integrate feedback from people outside the team. Exam tip: a log without owners and dates is only a list.

1.title: User Training and Acceptable Use
1.text: Training is by role: operators, reviewers, support staff and managers each need a different depth, as module two said. Article four asks deployers to take measures to support the development of A I literacy of the people who use the system. People given oversight of a high-risk system need competence, training and authority, under Article twenty-six. Write acceptable-use rules: what the tool is for, what it is not for, what data may go in, and how to report problems. Refresh the training after major changes and incidents. At Helios, recruiters learn why not to paste résumés into the assistant. Exam tip: training is a control.

1.title: Meaningful Human Oversight and Transparency to Users
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Meaningful oversight means the person can understand the system, interpret its output, and decide not to use, override or reverse it, under Article fourteen. Watch for automation bias: the habit of trusting the output too much. Provide a way to intervene or stop. For transparency, tell people they are interacting with A I, tell those exposed to emotion recognition under Article fifty, and tell affected people that a high-risk system supports decisions about them, under Article twenty-six. Measure override rates and review samples. Exam tip: oversight is meaningful only if people can disagree and act on it.

1.title: What the Deployer Monitors
1.text: The deployer watches the system in its own setting, with its own users and data. Six things to monitor. Outputs and accuracy against the thresholds from the impact assessment. Inputs and drift: shifts in who and what the system sees. Fairness of outcomes for your own groups. Feedback and overrides. Security and misuse: unusual queries, abuse and leakage. And provider changes: new versions, notices and incidents at the vendor. Exam tip: the deployer monitors the system in its own setting; the provider's monitoring cannot see that.

1.title: Maintenance, Updates and Retraining in Use
1.text: Changes come from two sources: the provider's and your own. Provider changes are new versions, patches and withdrawals; use the contract's notice and retest terms from module twelve. Your changes are prompts, settings, thresholds, knowledge sources, and any retraining or fine-tuning. Keep a schedule of regular reviews, patch windows and document refreshes, plus triggered changes after drift or incidents. Both sources pass through the same change control: test, approve, release in stages, monitor and roll back if needed. Record the version, settings and approver. Exam tip: every change, whoever makes it, gets the same routine.

1.title: Feedback and Escalation to the Provider
1.text: A deployer of a high-risk system must monitor operation and inform the provider, suspend use where there is a risk, and report any serious incident, under Article twenty-six. Use the contract: incident notice, support channels and service reviews. Share evidence, with privacy protected. Escalate inside: unresolved issues go to the business owner, then the committee. Track the provider's answers in the issue log. N I S T Manage four point three asks that incidents and errors are communicated to relevant A I actors, including affected communities. Exam tip: a quiet deployer loses both the fix and the chance to show diligence.

1.title: Periodic Checks: Schedule and Scope
1.text: Periodic checks step back from continuous monitoring and ask whether the system is still performing, reliable and safe in use. Set the schedule by risk, and also run checks after major changes. The table shows five: a metric review, a sample review, an impact assessment refresh, a security and misuse test, and a vendor review, each with its own rhythm. Owners run each check and report to the committee, and the results are kept even when nothing is found. At Helios, hiring-tool metrics are reviewed each quarter and assistant samples each month. Exam tip: monitoring watches; periodic checks test.

1.title: Audits and Reviews in Use
1.text: Audits and reviews give a backward look at evidence. Internal audit, the third line from module two, checks that the system in use follows policy and that controls work. Use the vendor's audit rights from module twelve, or ask for independent reports. Some laws require independent bias audits, such as New York City's rule for hiring tools, with a public summary. The scope covers policy compliance, training records, logs, issue and incident handling, and monitoring evidence. Findings get owners and due dates. At Helios, internal audit reviews hiring-tool oversight. Exam tip: an audit does not replace monitoring.

1.title: Red Teaming and Security Testing of Your Own Setup
1.text: The deployer's setup has its own weak points: system prompts, knowledge sources, connections and user habits. Red team your configuration: try misuse, injection through documents, data extraction and out-of-scope requests. Threat model new connections and features before they ship. Run security tests on access control, logging, data leakage and third-party components. Check reliability: failure handling, fallbacks to a person and recovery. And retest after every significant change. Exam tip: the provider's testing does not cover your configuration, so test it yourself.

1.title: Acting on Findings: Continue, Limit or Suspend
1.text: Every check ends in a decision: continue, continue with fixes, limit, or suspend. Severity decides: harm to people, legal duty and scale. Findings become actions with owners, dates and retests. Report results and trends to the business owner and the committee. Update the risk register, the impact assessment and the training. And remember that suspending use, where there is a risk, and informing the provider are required, under Article twenty-six. Exam tip: a check that never changes anything is not working.

2.title: Three Registers: Incidents, Issues and Risks in Use
2.text: Part two begins with records. Keep three registers. The incident register: every incident and near miss, with severity, cause, actions and closure. The issue log: problems found in use, with owner, due date and evidence of closure. The risk register: risks, likelihood, severity, controls, owners and status. Link them: an incident updates the risks, and repeated issues point to a risk. For the deployer's view, include provider incidents that affect you, and complaints from affected people. Review the registers at each committee meeting. Exam tip: what is not written down cannot be shown.

2.title: Logs and Retention
2.text: Automatic logs let you trace what the system did. Providers design logging in, under Article twelve, and deployers keep the logs under their control for at least six months, under Article twenty-six. Log inputs, outputs, versions, user actions, overrides and alerts. Protect the logs with access controls, because they may hold personal data. Balance retention: long enough for investigations and duties, and no longer than privacy rules allow. Use the logs for incident investigation, audits and monitoring. N I S T Manage four point three asks that incidents and errors are tracked and documented. Exam tip: logs serve oversight, but they can also be personal data.

2.title: Monitoring Plans: The Provider's Plan and the Deployer's Part
2.text: The provider runs a post-market monitoring system and plan for the product, under Article seventy-two, collecting and analyzing performance data over its lifetime. The deployer has its own part: it monitors operation and feeds information back to the provider, under Article twenty-six. Document your own monitoring plan: what is watched, by whom, thresholds, alerts, reviews and escalation. Align the two plans: who sends what to whom, how often and in which format. Update the plan when the system, the use or the risks change. Exam tip: the provider's plan covers the product; the deployer's plan covers the use.

2.title: Who Reports What to Whom
2.text: The table shows three reporting routes. When a high-risk system presents a risk or a serious incident, the deployer informs the provider, suspends use if there is a risk, and reports a serious incident, under Article twenty-six. When a provider has a serious incident, it reports to the market surveillance authority, under Article seventy-three, with the clocks from module ten. For a personal data breach, the controller notifies the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within seventy-two hours, under G D P R Article thirty-three. Contracts and sector rules may add shorter notices. Record who was told, when and what. Exam tip: the shortest applicable clock governs.

2.title: Secondary and Unintended Uses
2.text: A system approved for one purpose gets used for others. Learn four terms. Secondary use: a new purpose beyond the approved one. Unintended use: a use the builders did not foresee, often by well-meaning staff. Misuse: deliberate harmful use. And downstream harm: harm to people or systems that receive or rely on the output. At Helios, a recruiter ranking candidates with the customer assistant is an unintended use. N I S T also warns about off-label use of A I built for other purposes. Exam tip: most unintended use is not malicious; it is convenient.

2.title: Forecasting Misuse and Downstream Harm
2.text: To forecast, ask early: who else could use this system, for what, and what happens next? Use four lenses. The busy user who takes shortcuts. The curious user who tries everything. The bad actor who looks for abuse. And the downstream receiver who relies on the output. Methods include use-case workshops, pre-mortems, red teaming and scenario analysis. Evidence comes from query logs, feedback and shadow-use surveys. Add the forecast uses to the impact assessment, rate them by likelihood and severity, and plan controls. Exam tip: ask who else, for what, and what happens next.

2.title: Reducing the Risk: Scope, Access, Monitoring and Training
2.text: Reduce unintended use in five layers. Scope: state intended and out-of-scope uses, in the system and in the instructions. Access: least privilege, only the people and features that need it. Technical limits: system prompt limits, filters, blocked actions and rate limits. Monitoring: alerts for out-of-scope queries, and review of logs and shadow use. And people: training, user agreements and clear consequences. A change of purpose needs a new assessment, and a deployer that changes the intended purpose so that a system becomes high-risk is treated as its provider, under Article twenty-five, point one. Exam tip: say what the system is for and not for.

2.title: When Harm Travels Downstream
2.text: Downstream harm happens after the output leaves your system: a customer repeats a wrong answer, a partner reuses data, a decision rests on a draft. Mark outputs as A I-generated, with limits and the need to check. Add contract terms: license limits for partners and resellers, and no use for prohibited purposes. Track onward use where you can: A P I s, exports and shared datasets. N I S T lists value chain and component integration among the twelve generative A I risks. And fix and notify when downstream harm is found. Exam tip: responsibility does not stop at the output.

2.title: Who Needs to Hear What
2.text: An external communication plan says who is told what, when, by whom and through which channel. The table lists six audiences: users and customers, affected people, regulators and authorities, providers and partners, staff, and the public and media. Each needs different content, in plain language. Cover routine communication, such as notices, and event-driven communication, such as incidents, changes and shutdowns. Align the plan with legal duties and with the contract, and approve content with legal, privacy, communications and the business owner. Exam tip: plan the audiences first, then the messages.

2.title: Notices, Explanations and Incident Statements
2.text: Four parts of the content. Notices: people interacting with an A I system are told so, unless it is obvious, and deployers of emotion recognition inform the people exposed to it, under Article fifty. Explanations: what the system does, its limits, the role of human review, and how to ask for a person. An appeal and complaint route, with an owner and a response time. And incident statements: facts, impact, actions and the next update, prepared as templates with a holding statement. Promise nothing the system cannot deliver. Exam tip: prepare the words before the incident.

2.title: Running the Plan: Owners, Triggers, Channels and Rehearsal
2.text: The routine has five steps: trigger, decide, draft and approve, send, then log and follow up. Name one lead, with legal, privacy and communications. Set triggers: incidents above a set severity, regulator contact, major changes and public questions. Choose the right channel for each audience, within the required clocks. Rehearse with table-top exercises for an incident, a shutdown and a media question. Log what was said, to whom and when. At Helios, Samira Haddad, Jonas Weber and Anika Berg form the group. Exam tip: a plan that is never rehearsed will fail the first time.

2.title: Why Switch Off or Limit a System: The Triggers
2.text: To deactivate means to switch the system or one feature off. To localize means to limit it by region, group or feature. Six kinds of trigger. Regulatory: a prohibited practice in a region, a ban or an authority's order. Performance: accuracy or fairness below thresholds, or unsafe behavior. Incident and rights: a serious incident or a breach of people's rights. Supply: a vendor change or failure. And policy: use outside the approved scope. N I S T Manage two point four asks for mechanisms to supersede, disengage or deactivate. Exam tip: decide the triggers before launch, not during the crisis.

2.title: Deactivation Controls: Kill Switch, Pause and Fallback
2.text: Give yourself graded control. Feature flags turn one feature off without stopping everything. A pause stops new requests while the problem is studied. A kill switch is a tested way to stop the whole system at once. A fallback is a manual or older process so the business keeps running, with a person in the loop. And preserve evidence: logs, versions and data kept for investigation. Article fourteen expects a way to intervene or stop a high-risk system. Exam tip: a kill switch that has never been tested cannot be trusted.

2.title: Localizing a System by Region, Group or Feature
2.text: Laws and risks differ by region, user group and feature, so one setting rarely fits all. Four methods: regional switches, feature flags, user-group limits and data-location settings. Keep a map of each feature by region, with the legal reason and an owner. At Helios, the hiring tool's emotion analysis is off in the E U, because the law bans inferring emotions at work, under Article five, and it is limited by region elsewhere until legal review. Test that the switch holds, so that E U applicants never reach the feature. Exam tip: different settings in different places, with a record of why.

2.title: The Deactivation Policy: Authority, Steps and Records
2.text: The policy needs a named authority: who may order a shutdown, including out of hours, and who must be told. It sets clear criteria and a fast route for urgent cases. The steps are: decide, act, verify that it worked, notify, and investigate. Notify users, affected people, the provider and authorities as required. Keep records of the decision, the time, the reason and who acted. And test the policy with exercises that include switching off and recovering. Exam tip: nobody should need a meeting to stop a harm.

2.title: After Deactivation: Retire, Retain and Restart
2.text: Switching off starts a process. Decide the outcome: restart after fixes, run in a limited form, or retire the system. Restart only when the root cause is fixed, retests have passed, approvals are given and communication is done. To retire, stop access, archive the model and documents, and delete or transfer data under privacy rules and contracts; N I S T names decommissioning in Manage four point one. Retain logs and records for the periods that law and policy require. Tell users and partners what ends and what replaces it. And learn: update the policy, the tests and the training. Exam tip: decide whether to restart, limit or retire.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Let us recap. Policies in use: a named owner, training, issue management, data governance and a live risk register, with oversight that is meaningful. Monitoring and checks: the deployer's own monitoring, change control for provider and own changes, and periodic checks that end in a decision. Records and reporting: three registers, logs for at least six months, monitoring plans and reporting routes. Unintended use: four lenses to forecast, five layers to reduce. Communication: audiences, notices, templates and rehearsal. And switching off: triggers, kill switch, fallback, localizing, a policy with named authority, and restart or retire.

3.title: Practice Question 1
3.text: Question one. Lucia Moreno's recruiters approve almost every candidate ranking that the Helios hiring tool produces, usually within seconds, and have never overridden one. What is the best governance response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Near-total agreement and no overrides can signal automation bias. Measure the oversight, train the recruiters and give them time to challenge.

3.title: Practice Question 2
3.text: Question two. A company puts a customer-facing generative A I assistant into use. Which two actions apply its policies to the system in use? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and D. Applying policy in use means accountable ownership, an issue route, rules for inputs and managed knowledge sources. A press release, waiting for complaints and no training apply no policy.

3.title: Practice Question 3
3.text: Question three. A company uses a vendor's language model through an interface. The vendor announces a new model version for next month. What should the company do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Provider changes are changes to your system. Test the new version before it reaches users, approve it under change control and keep a rollback ready.

3.title: Practice Question 4
3.text: Question four. Which is the best example of a periodic check by the deployer, as distinct from continuous monitoring? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Periodic checks step back and test the system on a schedule: sample review, fairness retest and assessment refresh. Alerts, dashboards and automatic logs are continuous monitoring.

3.title: Practice Question 5
3.text: Question five. A deployer of a high-risk A I system keeps the automatically generated logs that are under its control. What is the best statement about how long to keep them? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Deployers keep the logs they control for at least six months, and because logs can contain personal data, privacy limits apply as well.

3.title: Practice Question 6
3.text: Question six. A Helios recruiter pastes candidates' résumés into the customer assistant and asks it to rank them. The assistant was approved only for answering customers' questions about services. What describes this situation and the best response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. It is an unintended use outside the approved scope. Stop it, restate the scope, add controls, and assess the hiring risk.

3.title: Practice Question 7
3.text: Question seven. Which two methods help forecast secondary or unintended uses of an A I system? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and E. Forecasting asks who else might use the system, and checks how it is really used, through workshops, pre-mortems, red teaming and log review. Assuming compliance, waiting for regulators and counting pages forecast nothing.

3.title: Practice Question 8
3.text: Question eight. Samira Haddad asks for an external communication plan for the Helios assistant. Which element is most important to prepare before any incident occurs? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A plan works when it has owners, triggers, channels and prepared templates for each audience, and has been rehearsed. Promising no errors, one message for everyone and silence are not plans.

3.title: Practice Question 9
3.text: Question nine. The Helios hiring tool includes an emotion-analysis feature that is unlawful for E U applicants but may be usable elsewhere after legal review. Which control best localizes the system? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Localizing means different settings in different places: switch the feature off in the E U, test the switch and record why. A notice does not make a prohibited use lawful.

3.title: Practice Question 10
3.text: Question ten. A company drafts a policy to deactivate a high-risk A I system when needed. Which two elements belong in it? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and E. A deactivation policy needs a named authority with clear triggers, and steps to notify, preserve evidence and record. Committee meetings for urgent events, an untested kill switch and a promise never to switch off defeat the purpose.

3.title: Answers at a Glance
3.text: Here are all ten answers. Question one: C. Question two: A and D. Question three: D. Question four: B. Question five: A. Question six: C. Question seven: B and E. Question eight: D. Question nine: A. Question ten: C and E. That completes Module thirteen, and with it domain four. Next, Module fourteen is a quick-reference recap of everything so far, and Module fifteen covers exam technique.
